## Chords on the blues scale

Tom Sutcliffe builds a chord on each note of the blues scale: I7♯9, ♭IIImaj7, IV7, ♯IV°7, V7♯9,
♭VII7. All their notes (or nearly all) come from the scale.

<div class="bz" data-w="chords" data-set="bluesscale" data-title="Chords on the blues scale"></div>

## Diminished chords

A **I°7** (a diminished 7th on the key note) is common in blues. Hein's example is Robert
Johnson's *Kind Hearted Woman Blues*, which goes back and forth between I7 and I°7. I°7 has
three of the four notes of IV7, and all its notes are in the blues or major blues scale. The
turnaround I7 – ii7 – ♯ii°7 – I7 (or the reverse) is another common use.

<div class="bz" data-w="chords" data-set="dim" data-title="I°7 and the turnaround"></div>

## ♭VI7, the minor blues subdominant

♭VI7 (A♭7 in C): its root is not in the blues scale, but its other notes are. Jaffe calls it the
minor blues subdominant. It works in major or minor tunes. Hein's example is John Coltrane's
*Equinox*.

<div class="bz" data-w="chords" data-set="bvi" data-title="♭VI7"></div>

## The Hendrix chord: home, not dominant

A dominant 7♯9 chord holds a major 3rd and, an octave up, a minor 3rd (written as a ♯9).
Charalampidis gives it two jobs. One is a **V7♯9** that resolves to I. The other is a
**home chord** whose two 3rds express the blue 3rd's area, which he would spell I7♭10. He gives a
John Lee Hooker recording as an example of the same sound split between instruments: a guitar
on E7 and a piano on Em7 an octave above. (He plays the recording in part 9 of his series. The
spoken text does not name the song.)

<div class="bz" data-w="chords" data-set="hendrix" data-title="One chord, two jobs"></div>

## "Avoid notes" that are not avoided

In jazz teaching, the 4th of a dominant chord is an **avoid note**: F over C7 clashes with the
E. Hein's example is Albert Collins's *Don't Lose Your Cool*, in F. Collins keeps playing F,
the key note, even over C7, and it sounds right. Hein calls the blues scale a "universal
harmonic solvent" that sounds right over any chord (citing Mark Levine). He rejects the idea that blues melody and harmony are "divorced"
(Temperley): there *are* rules, just different ones.

Set every bar to **Key note only** and play. The band plays a 12-bar in your key while the lead
holds the key note through every chord, the V7 included.

<div class="bz" data-w="chorus" data-form="major" data-plan="root,root,root,root,root,root,root,root,root,root,root,root" data-title="The key note over every chord"></div>

## Is this "dissonance"?

Hein collects the ways theorists describe blues notes from outside:

- McClary: blues values sounds that classically trained ears hear as "out of tune".
- Everett: blues tritones and half steps are "intrinsically dissonant".
- Wagner: blue notes are "alienated" until they are "domesticated".
- Tymoczko: blues as a source of jazz "playing out".

Hein's answer is that no blues player thinks they are playing wrong notes. A dominant 7th home
chord is consonant inside blues tonality. **Discuss:** what changes when you call a sound
"dissonant" rather than "from another system"?
